ratings.reason: Synchronized video comments fit the basic timing pattern, but the quote describes danmaku generally rather than showing how ClassComet generates or schedules its own comments. The design may be useful educationally, but impact and novelty are not judgeable beyond the title and this background-level evidence.

Real-time musical cooperation makes latency constitutive: an AI contribution arriving after the musical moment is unusable. Low latency, communicating planned actions, and adapting continuously are unusually clear requirements, though transfer beyond tightly coupled performance is somewhat limited.

Speech is continuously tracked and proactive gesture cues appear during the relevant rehearsal moment, closely matching the structural signature. The interaction is highly rebuildable and consequential for rehearsal, although live coaching cues are a fairly established design move.

Speech-to-text and RSVP output in a live sales stream plausibly require synchronization, and the accessibility stakes are substantial. The quote does not specify item-level timing, latency, or how LLM simplifications remain aligned with their referents, so the pattern fit is only moderately supported.

A collaboratively updated dialogue map during an ongoing meeting is a clean continuous-output instance. The quote makes the live interaction legible but does not show the latency policy or whether individual map additions are tied to particular utterances; real-time meeting mapping is now competent rather than surprising.

The pre-call/during-call/post-call contrast makes intervention timing the central design move: a warning must arrive while the scam can still be interrupted. This addresses a serious breakdown and generalizes to other live risk detection, though the truncated quote leaves the exact warning presentation unspecified.

Real-time issue mapping consumes an unfolding discussion and updates a knowledge representation before the meeting ends. It is broadly transferable facilitation infrastructure, but the evidence does not explain update granularity, scheduling, or latency, and live discussion maps are no longer a radical move.

Generating visual material synchronously with verbal communication is an exceptionally clean case where late output loses its referent. Extending captions from text into heterogeneous visuals materially expands the design space and transfers across conversation, teaching, and presentation, although the quote omits implementation-level scheduling detail.

The supplied quote establishes automatic transcription and annotation but says nothing about when annotations are generated or shown. Automatic processing could equally be deferred until after the discussion, so the evidence does not support this timing pattern.
ratings.disqualify_reason: The evidence quote does not support live or referent-synchronized output.

ratings.reason: Knowledge flashcards appear while a video plays, making this a clear no-batch support pipeline with a readily transferable side-panel mechanism. The quote does not demonstrate that each flashcard is aligned to the precise jargon occurrence, and real-time contextual explanation is a comparatively settled idea.

The virtual fencer updates immediately when the audience moves, so timing is observable and technically supported. However, this is closer to continuous embodied control or reactive animation than scheduling discrete informational outputs against referents in an independent activity; its novelty lies more in the installation than in this pattern.

An assistant synchronized with live gameplay squarely invokes the pattern, since spoiler-aware help depends on current narrative state. The evidence does not say what events trigger output, what appears, or how synchronization is maintained, making impact and mechanism difficult to assess confidently.

The quote indicates synchronized AI visuals and narration during walking, an intriguing coupling of media with everyday activity. It is ambiguous whether outputs track the independently unfolding walk or merely synchronize with one another while the user walks, and the specialized assisted-reality setup limits direct transfer.

Real-time emotional captions embedded in a conferencing camera feed are a clear live-output mechanism. The virtual-camera packaging is reusable, but the quote does not explicitly connect each caption to a contemporaneous utterance or emotion, and live caption augmentation is fairly incremental.

Graphologue incrementally constructs a diagram as the source response streams, almost exactly instantiating the structural signature. The coupling is concrete, transferable to many streams, and meaningfully changes how users can inspect generation before completion; streaming visualization was a notable design-space move.

Transforming a child's spoken telling into drawings as the telling unfolds makes timing central to collaborative storytelling. The move is memorable and materially changes children's ability to externalize stories, though the short quote leaves the exact alignment and correction interaction unspecified.

Live lecture transcription is synchronized output, but the quoted feature is ordinary speech-to-text and appears incidental to AskNow's larger question-answering contribution. It transfers broadly, yet the supplied evidence does not show synchronized answers or another distinctive timing mechanism.

Updating instructor-authored slides during a live discussion is a consequential and relatively unusual way to keep shared material aligned with conversation. However, the quote says the system enables semantic updates rather than showing continuous consumption, automatic scheduling, or exact referent alignment.

Adapting an interview script to the ongoing conversation is timing-sensitive support that can affect follow-up quality while an opportunity still exists. The adaptive-script and progress/balance display are legible and transferable, but the malformed quote gives little evidence about triggers, latency, or evaluation.

A visualization that evolves during a meeting is compatible with continuous synchronized output, but the quote does not identify its input items, update triggers, or connection between an update and its referent. Meeting-progress visualization is useful but, on this evidence, conventional.

Continuous smiley or numeric feedback while a child speaks fits the no-batch timing requirement and could improve responses before they are finalized. The feedback forms are concrete, although the quote does not say which properties of speech drive each update or demonstrate precise referent synchronization.

Discussion is summarized into sticky notes and shared on a whiteboard in real time, a very clear and rebuildable live-output pipeline. It generalizes well, but automatic meeting summaries placed on collaborative canvases are now a heavily explored, derivative design move, and item-level latency is not described.

Extracting key information and entities from verbal discussion in real time is a clean streaming augmentation with broad transfer to collaborative settings. It could substantially reduce group sensemaking effort, but the quote does not specify the presentation, latency, or exact binding between entities and utterances.

Real-time skill–evidence mapping creates interview support while questions can still be adapted, making timing operationally important. The mapping mechanism is intelligible and transferable to other assessment conversations, though it is one feature among several and appears evolutionary rather than field-shifting.

Emotion-tailored interventions delivered during gameplay are valuable only while the detected rage state and regulating opportunity remain current. This is an interesting use of synchronized intervention with plausible wellbeing impact, but the quote omits sensing triggers and output form, and transfer depends on reliable affect inference.

Rational interventions during live commerce target the narrow moment before persuasion becomes a purchase, so late delivery would undermine the design. Product comparison and speech reframing are concrete and consequential, though the quote does not establish event-level alignment and the mechanism is tied to transactional streams.

Humorous AAC contributions have an unusually strict conversational timing window: even good content becomes socially wrong when late. Generating contextually relevant suggestions in real time addresses a genuine participation limitation and reframes live assistance around social timing, though the evidence says the authors consider multiple designs rather than documenting one exact scheduler.

Matching interface panels to ongoing conversation can surface tools or context at relevant moments and is a broadly reusable substrate. The quote only describes relevance matching; it does not explicitly say that matched material is emitted immediately or specify latency and presentation behavior.

In-the-moment verbalization prompts and low-distraction feedback accompany an unfolding think-aloud work process, making intervention timing visible and important. Pointer-centric grounding is an interesting extension, but the supplied evidence does not describe triggering, temporal alignment, or demonstrated outcome shifts.

Real-time coupling of nonvisual cues with visual information during cooking plausibly delivers assistance while each physical state is actionable, with exceptionally high accessibility and safety stakes. The quote does not specify what output is emitted, what event it refers to, or its latency, and the multimodal cooking setup constrains direct generalization.
